claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure.
The hierarchical heterostructure contains multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A physics-constrained, microstructure-informed surrogate can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness for hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10.
The surrogate can achieve predictions within approximately 10% of experimental measurements.
The surrogate can reduce computational cost relative to full-scale CALPHAD, first-principles, and unstructured machine-learning methods.
The proposed framework combines limited high-fidelity first-principles calculations, unsupervised descriptor extraction, and physics-informed regression or neural networks.
Chemical-segregation scales, domain sizes, and interphase-boundary characteristics mediate local stress distributions.
Chemical-segregation scales, domain sizes, and interphase-boundary characteristics mediate deformation mechanisms.
Lower-dimensional statistical descriptors can retain the microstructural heterogeneities relevant to mechanical response.
Energy-conservation and stress-continuity constraints allow a model trained on limited high-fidelity data to predict overall mechanical response.
Using distilled microstructural descriptors bypasses the need for full high-fidelity simulations.
Local microstructural variations govern ductility and toughness.
The proposed model is expected to improve computational efficiency by a factor of 5–10.
The proposed model may reduce prediction error by approximately 10–20% relative to prior standalone methods.
CALPHAD, first-principles calculations, and standard machine-learning approaches require extensive computational resources.
Prior standalone methods have larger predictive uncertainties, particularly for fracture toughness.
The model assumes that the hierarchical structure remains stable without phase transformation or significant degradation during testing.
Thermal excursions, non-equilibrium processing, or microstructural damage can make the model unreliable by invalidating its descriptors.
Unrepresented mechanisms such as phase transformations or emergent slip systems at extreme strain rates can cause substantial prediction errors.
The quantitative targets are based on analogous successes in similar alloy systems and preliminary model validations.
